name: Team Dresch
label: Chainsaw
lede: A zine, two labels and one 16-year-old's letter turned into a queercore band that booked its first tour over AOL and printed Mariel Hemingway, mid-hurdle, on its T-shirts.

eras.title: Letters first, band second
eras.text: Before the band there was Donna Dresch's zine Chainsaw and a queercore scene held together by mail. Kaia Wilson wrote to Dresch at 16, Jody Bleyle was already running Candy Ass Records, and the four who became Team Dresch booked a first tour on AOL message boards.

years.h: Donna Dresch fills in on bass for Dinosaur Jr.
years.p: The 1990 tour ran across the US and Australia, three years before Team Dresch existed.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists the Dinosaur Jr. stint alongside a stretch as a temporary replacement in [[Screaming Trees|bc5e6e42-73ba-44fa-a41e-3379402f0429]]. Next to the gigs she was making Chainsaw, and writing for Outpunk, Homocore and Tobi Vail's Jigsaw.

years.big: "We booked the whole tour in 1993 on the internet, which most people didn't know what the thing was."
years.src: OPB: Pioneering Northwest punk band · Vortex: Team Dresch Remember Who They Are · Wikipedia: Team Dresch
years.h: Team Dresch forms in Olympia, or Portland, depending who you ask
years.p: Jody Bleyle, to OPB. Wikipedia puts Donna Dresch, Bleyle, Kaia Wilson and Marcéo Martinez in Olympia in 1993; Vortex says Portland in 1994.
years.xp:
Wilson found Dresch through the zines. OPB says she saw Chainsaw's ad asking "Are you a misfit dork dyke?" and wrote at 16. Dresch and Bleyle met backstage after a Hazel show at the Capitol Theater in Olympia, where Bleyle suggested a band. Bleyle was already drumming in Hazel and running Candy Ass; Dresch had started Chainsaw Records in the early 1990s.

The AOL tour leaned on colleges, Bleyle says, because those were the only people with email addresses. Vortex has Wilson on the shirt art, Mariel Hemingway hurdling from the film Personal Best: "None of us could do that but we had the will."

eras.title: Five days in Seattle
eras.text: A seven-inch on Kill Rock Stars got the band a national tour. A debut LP recorded in five days came out on Chainsaw and Candy Ass, the two labels run by two of its members.

years.src: Wikipedia: Team Dresch · Vortex: Team Dresch Remember Who They Are
years.h: A 7-inch on Kill Rock Stars, then a tour of the whole country
years.p: The single carries "Hand Grenade" on one side, with "Endtime Relay" and "Molasses in January" on the other.
years.xp: Wikipedia says the band's track "Seven" on a Rock Stars Kill compilation drew enough attention for a national tour. Vortex adds that Rolling Stone wrote it up kindly. Wilson's version: "It was boom, we hit the ground running and we're gone."

years.h: John Goodmanson gets five days with ten songs
years.p: In August 1994 the band records Personal Best at Avast! in Seattle, then goes home and starts mailing it out.
years.xp: Wikipedia's page on the album gives August 1994 and Avast! in Seattle. The finished record runs about 24 minutes.

years.src: Wikipedia: Personal Best · Wikipedia: Team Dresch
years.h: Personal Best comes out on two labels the band runs itself
years.p: Released January 23, 1995 on Chainsaw (Dresch) and Candy Ass (Bleyle). Its ten tracks include "Hate the Christian Right!" and "Freewheel".
years.xp:
AllMusic's Jason Ankeny wrote that it "explodes on contact." The Washington Post called it "a fiery, all-but-forgotten punk masterpiece." Wikipedia says it had sold more than 20,000 copies by 2004, and Rolling Stone placed it at number 48 on a 2026 list of greatest punk albums.

The title nods to the 1982 lesbian-themed film of the same name.

years.src: Bandcamp Daily: The Power of Community · Wikipedia: Candy Ass Records
years.h: Jody Bleyle puts a self-defense manual inside a double LP
years.p: Free to Fight on Candy Ass collects all-women bands and ships with a 75-page booklet of self-defense advice. The band carries the idea out on the road.
years.xp:
Bandcamp Daily ties the project to Bleyle's own experience: a club owner attacked her after the band's first show, and she decided to get information to people through records.

According to Wikipedia's Candy Ass page the label's other artists included [[Sleater-Kinney|e36e78eb-3ace-4acd-882c-16789e700ab7]], [[Excuse 17|bad37a2a-1ab8-4605-b8f3-e0615cd7de64]], [[Heavens to Betsy|8716a313-c6df-440c-9b74-370e8d79728e]] and Hazel. Its promised singles series ended after one release, a Sleater-Kinney and Cypher in the Snow split, because of money.

eras.title: A new drummer, a harder record, a blow-up
eras.text: Melissa York took over the drums and the band made Captain My Captain. By the end of that tour the original line-up had come apart, and Wilson and York left to start The Butchies.

years.src: Wikipedia: Team Dresch · Wikipedia: Melissa York · OPB: Pioneering Northwest punk band
years.h: Melissa York comes over from New York hardcore
years.p: She takes the drum stool from Marcéo Martinez for the second album, after time in Born Against.
years.xp:
Wikipedia's Melissa York page lists Born Against, The Manacled and Vitapup among her earlier bands, and dates her Team Dresch years to 1993 onward; the band's own page puts her replacing Martinez in 1996.

OPB's interview has Scott Plouff of Spinanes as the band's very first drummer, before Martinez.

years.h: Bleyle writes through a breakdown and Captain My Captain is the result
years.p: Released June 4, 1996 and recorded at John and Stu's Place in Seattle. Bleyle says much of her writing came from a physical and emotional breakdown before the sessions.
years.xp:
The album came out on Chainsaw and Candy Ass with John Goodmanson producing again. It has eleven songs, including "Uncle Phranc" for the folk singer Phranc, who guests, and "Don't Try Suicide." It closes on "Remember Who You Are," over eight minutes long. Pitchfork later scored it 8.8 out of 10.

Wikipedia describes it as a more outwardly queer record than Personal Best, with mental health in the frame.

years.src: Wikipedia: Team Dresch · Discogs: Team Dresch / Bikini Kill
yt: Full set, Morse Dining Hall, Yale, March 3, 1996
years.h: Bikini Kill and Team Dresch put a spring tour on a 7-inch
years.p: The split single is named for the band's Spring Tour 1996 with [[Bikini Kill|1397d045-1603-41fc-80b9-712c18360145]]. One of the tour's stops is a Yale dining hall on March 3.
years.xp: It was one of several splits the band made that year; Wikipedia also lists "What Can a Lover Do?" with F-80, Shove and Dahlia Seed on Marigold Records. The clip is the full Yale set, filmed in Morse Dining Hall.

years.src: Wikipedia: Team Dresch · Wikipedia: Candy Ass Records
years.h: On camera in She's Real (Worse Than Queer)
years.p: Lucy Thane's documentary on riot grrrl and queercore films the band, and Bleyle also talks about Candy Ass and Free to Fight.

years.big: "A big blow up that no one in the group likes to talk about in any detail."
years.src: Vortex: Team Dresch Remember Who They Are · Wikipedia: The Butchies · Wikipedia: Kaia Wilson · Wikipedia: Team Dresch
years.h: Kaia Wilson and Melissa York leave for North Carolina and start The Butchies
years.p: Vortex's description of how the original line-up ended. The Butchies' first album, Are We Not Femme?, arrives the same year.
years.xp:
Vortex says Bleyle and Dresch had been a couple early on, which added strain to long drives between tour stops, and that the original line-up imploded after a tour. Wilson had already co-founded Mr. Lady Records with Tammy Rae Carland in 1996, and The Butchies' first three albums came out on it.

The band's last release of the first run was The New Team Dresch V 6.0 Beta, a 7-inch on Outpunk.

eras.title: Back, a few shows at a time
eras.text: The band returned for a festival in Olympia and kept coming back in short runs, on its own schedule.

years.cap: Team Dresch playing to a packed pit, July 2007
years.h: Six years after splitting, Team Dresch headlines Homo-a-Go-Go
years.p: Olympia's queercore festival gets the band back in 2004, and the shows keep coming in short runs afterward.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists sporadic West and East Coast tours in 2006 and 2007, an appearance at Outfest in California, Pacific Northwest shows in 2009 and 2014, and two shows at Ladyfest in Brazil in May 2010. The band describes its approach since as taking things day by day.

years.h: Team Dresch lands in a queercore documentary
years.p: Yony Leyser's Queercore: How to Punk a Revolution features the band alongside the scene that made them.
years.xp: Wikipedia's Team Dresch page lists the appearance.

eras.title: The catalogue comes home
eras.text: Jealous Butcher reissued everything for the 25th anniversary, the band played Portland for Pride weekend and put out its first new song in 19 years. Since then it has tended to the catalogue and who gets credit in it.

years.src: Vortex: Team Dresch Remember Who They Are · Wikipedia: Team Dresch
yt: "Fagetarian and Dyke," video from unseen live footage
Live at the Bootleg Theater, Los Angeles, June 21, 2019
years.h: Twenty-five years on, the whole catalogue is back in print
years.p: Jealous Butcher Records reissues both albums and the singles collection Choices, Chances, Changes on May 31, 2019.
years.xp:
Vortex says Jealous Butcher's Rob Jones asked to do it, and Dresch's account is that the band said okay. Two Portland shows at Mississippi Studios, June 14 and 15, marked Pride weekend.

Marcéo Martinez came out publicly as transmasculine that year, and the reissued credits were corrected; Wikipedia quotes him calling that "so important and necessary" for visibility.

years.big: "Your music stopped me from killing myself."
years.src: Bandcamp Daily: The Power of Community · Wikipedia: Team Dresch
yt: Women of Rock Oral History Project, 2018
years.h: A new single, 19 years after the last one
years.p: Melissa York told Bandcamp Daily the band gets letters from kids that say this. "Your Hands My Pockets" is the 2019 single.
years.xp: The same year brought a new video for "Fagetarian and Dyke" made from previously unseen live footage. Wilson told Bandcamp Daily the band had been pretty inactive and had decided to get more active, which Bandcamp Daily framed as less a reunion than a return to work.

years.h: "Story of the Earth" sends its money to the Trans Justice Funding Project
years.p: Written in 2007 after colony collapse disorder made the news. All proceeds from the July 2020 single go to the fund.

years.h: Oregon Music Hall of Fame takes them in
years.p: Wikipedia's Donna Dresch page dates the induction to 2023.

years.src: OPB: Pioneering Northwest punk band · Bandcamp Daily: The Power of Community
years.p: OPB has the band out on an anniversary tour, with both Martinez and York among the drummers.
years.xp: Wilson told Bandcamp Daily in 2019 that she thinks a five-piece, with both drummers, "is how I think it should be for all of eternity."
